title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
summary: What asteroids are, why most of them orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter, how they differ from icy comets, and how scientists track the ones that pass near Earth.
poll: Scientists should spend a lot of money tracking asteroids that pass near Earth.

versions.title: Rocky Leftovers in Space
versions.text:
Space is not empty. It has planets and moons. It has rocks too. Some rocks move around the sun. We call them asteroids.

Long ago, bits of rock tried to join. Most did not grow big. They did not grow into a planet. They stayed as small bits.

Most of them sit in one spot. It sits between Mars and Jupiter. We call this spot the belt. So many rocks sit there!

A comet is not the same as a rock like this. A comet is mostly ice. Near the sun, a comet can grow a long, bright tail. A plain rock does not grow a tail like that.

A few rocks drift away from the belt. Some come near Earth. We watch the sky with big scopes. We track these rocks. We want to know if one will come too close.

These rocks may look small. But they teach us a lot. They are bits left from when our solar system first formed.

These rocks may look small and plain. But they can teach us a great deal. They are leftover bits from when our whole solar system first formed.

versions.title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
versions.text:
Space is not empty at all. It is full of planets, moons, and other things too. One of these things is a large kind of rock. We call this rock an asteroid. It moves around the sun, much like a planet does. But it is far smaller and has no round shape.

Long ago, our solar system was still forming. Small bits of rock and metal tried to join together. Most of these bits never grew big enough to form a true planet. They stayed small instead, as the rocks we now call asteroids.

Most of these rocks float together in one crowded area. We call this area the asteroid belt. It lies between the planets Mars and Jupiter. Scientists think there are millions of rocks packed into this one belt alone. Most are far too small to see without a telescope, though.

Many people think a comet is the same as one of these rocks. But they are not the same at all. A rock like this is made mostly of stone and metal. A comet, though, is made mostly of ice mixed with dust. When a comet gets close to the sun, its ice heats up. It can grow a long, glowing tail that stretches out behind it. A plain rock almost never grows a tail like this. It simply has far too little ice.

A few of these rocks drift away from the belt. Some come close to Earth's own path through space. Scientists use strong telescopes to watch the sky closely. They track these wandering rocks. They check whether one might ever come too close to us.

These rocks may look small and rather plain. But they can teach us a great deal about the past. They are leftover building blocks from when our whole solar system first formed, billions of years ago.

versions.title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
versions.text:
Space may look empty, but it is full of planets, moons, and countless smaller objects too. One kind of object is an asteroid. An asteroid is a chunk of rock that orbits the sun, much like a planet does. But it is far smaller and has no rounded shape.

Asteroids never managed to grow into full planets. Long ago, our solar system was still forming. Small fragments of rock and metal tried to clump together under the pull of gravity. Most of these fragments never grew large enough to form a true planet. So they stayed small instead.

Most known asteroids orbit together in one crowded region. We call this region the asteroid belt. It lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Scientists estimate that millions of asteroids occupy this one belt. Most are far too small to see without a telescope, though.

Many people confuse asteroids with comets, but they are quite different things. An asteroid consists mostly of rock and metal, with very little ice. A comet, on the other hand, is made mostly of ice and dust. When a comet gets close enough to the sun, its ice can vaporize. This can form a long, glowing tail behind it. Asteroids almost never grow a tail like this, since they simply lack enough ice.

Some asteroids eventually drift out of the main belt. A few of these can come close enough to Earth's orbit. Scientists worry that one might someday collide with our planet. Astronomers use powerful telescopes to track these wandering rocks and calculate their paths.

Though asteroids may look small and plain, they can teach scientists a great deal. They preserve material from the solar system's distant past.

versions.title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
versions.text:
Space may appear empty, but it is actually populated by planets, moons, and countless smaller celestial bodies, including asteroids. An asteroid is a fragment of rock, frequently combined with metal, that orbits the sun much as a planet does. It is far smaller, though, and lacks the rounded shape that larger worlds acquire from their own gravity.

Asteroids never managed to coalesce into full, rounded planets. Long ago, while the solar system was still taking shape, countless small fragments of rock and metal attempted to clump together under gravity's steady pull. Most of these fragments never grew large enough to form a true planet, in part because Jupiter's gravitational pull kept stirring and scattering them.

Most known asteroids orbit together within one especially crowded region, the asteroid belt, located between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Scientists estimate that millions of individual asteroids occupy this single belt, though most are far too small to observe without a powerful telescope.

Many people confuse asteroids with comets, yet these are fundamentally different kinds of objects. Asteroids consist mostly of rock and metal, with very little ice, whereas comets are made mostly of ice mixed with dust, often called dirty snowballs. When a comet travels close to the sun, its ice vaporizes and forms a long, glowing tail. Asteroids almost never grow a tail like this, since they simply lack enough ice.

Some asteroids drift out of the main belt, and a few of these, formally called near-Earth objects, can come close enough to collide with our planet someday. Astronomers run dedicated survey programs with powerful telescopes to track these wandering bodies and calculate their paths.

Though asteroids may look small from a distance, they teach scientists a great deal about the solar system's distant past, since their material has remained largely unchanged for billions of years.

versions.title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
versions.text:
Space may appear empty, but it is actually populated by planets, moons, and countless smaller celestial bodies, including asteroids. An asteroid is a fragment of rock, frequently combined with metal, that orbits the sun much as a planet does, though on a considerably smaller scale and lacking the rounded shape that larger worlds acquire through their own sustained gravitational force.

Asteroids never managed to coalesce into full, rounded planets during the solar system's formative history. Billions of years ago, while the solar system was still actively taking shape from a swirling disk of gas and dust, countless small fragments of rock and metal attempted to clump together under gravity's steady, persistent pull. Most of these fragments never grew sufficiently large to form a genuine planet, in part because Jupiter's considerable gravitational influence repeatedly stirred and scattered the fragments before they could ever merge further.

Most known asteroids orbit together within one especially crowded region, the asteroid belt, situated between the respective orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Scientists estimate that millions of individual asteroids occupy this single belt, though most remain far too small to observe without a sufficiently powerful telescope, and their combined mass is still considerably less than the mass of Earth's own moon.

Many people mistakenly confuse asteroids with comets, yet these represent fundamentally different categories of celestial objects. Asteroids consist predominantly of solid rock and metal, with very little ice, whereas comets are composed primarily of ice mixed with dust, often described informally as dirty snowballs. When a comet travels sufficiently close to the sun, its ice vaporizes rapidly, producing a long, glowing tail that stretches out dramatically behind it. Asteroids almost never develop a tail of this kind, since they simply lack sufficient ice to vaporize in this manner.

Some asteroids eventually drift out of the main belt entirely, and a number of these, formally classified as near-Earth objects, can approach dangerously close to our planet's orbital path. Astronomers worldwide operate dedicated survey programs with powerful telescopes to continuously track these wandering bodies and calculate their precise orbits.

Though asteroids may appear small and rather unremarkable from a considerable distance, they teach scientists a tremendous amount about the solar system's distant past, since their material has remained largely unchanged for billions of years since the solar system itself first formed.

versions.title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
versions.text:
Space may appear empty, but it is in fact populated by planets, moons, and countless smaller celestial bodies, including asteroids; an asteroid is a fragment of rock, frequently combined with metal, that orbits the sun much as a planet does, though on a considerably smaller scale and lacking the rounded shape larger worlds acquire through their own sustained gravitational force over immense spans of time.

Asteroids never managed to coalesce into full, rounded planets during the solar system's formative history. Billions of years ago, while the solar system was still taking shape from a swirling disk of gas and dust, countless small fragments of rock and metal attempted to clump together under gravity's steady pull; most never grew sufficiently large to form a genuine planet, in part because Jupiter's considerable gravitational influence repeatedly stirred and scattered the fragments before they could ever merge further together.

Most known asteroids orbit together within one especially crowded region, the asteroid belt, situated between the respective orbits of Mars and Jupiter; scientists estimate millions of individual asteroids occupy this single belt, though most remain far too small to observe without a sufficiently powerful telescope, and their combined mass is still far less than the mass of Earth's own moon.

Many people mistakenly confuse asteroids with comets, yet these represent fundamentally different categories of celestial objects. Asteroids consist predominantly of solid rock and metal, with very little ice, whereas comets are composed primarily of ice mixed with dust, often described informally as dirty snowballs; when a comet travels sufficiently close to the sun, its ice vaporizes rapidly, producing a long, glowing tail that stretches dramatically behind it, while asteroids almost never develop a tail of this kind, since they simply lack sufficient ice to vaporize in such a manner.

Some asteroids eventually drift out of the main belt entirely, and a number of these, formally classified as near-Earth objects, can approach dangerously close to our planet's orbital path; astronomers worldwide operate dedicated survey programs with powerful telescopes to continuously track these wandering bodies, calculating their precise orbits years or even decades before any potential close approach to Earth.

Though asteroids may appear small and rather unremarkable from a considerable distance, they teach scientists a tremendous amount about the solar system's distant past, since their material has remained largely unchanged for billions of years since the solar system itself first formed, offering scientists a rare and valuable glimpse of the raw material from which the planets, including our own Earth, were originally assembled long ago.

versions.title: Asteroids: Rocky Leftovers of the Solar System
versions.text:
Space may appear empty at first glance, but it is in fact densely populated by planets, moons, and countless smaller celestial bodies, including asteroids; an asteroid is a fragment of rock, frequently combined with metal, that orbits the sun much as a planet does, though on a considerably smaller scale and lacking the rounded shape that larger worlds typically acquire through their own sustained gravitational force over immense spans of time.

Asteroids never managed to coalesce into full, rounded planets during the solar system's formative history. Billions of years ago, while the solar system was still actively taking shape from a swirling disk of gas and dust, countless small fragments of rock and metal attempted to clump together under gravity's steady, persistent pull; most never grew sufficiently large to form a genuine planet, in large part because Jupiter's considerable gravitational influence repeatedly stirred and scattered these fragments before they could ever merge further together.

Most known asteroids orbit together within one especially crowded region, the asteroid belt, situated between the respective orbits of Mars and Jupiter; scientists estimate that millions of individual asteroids occupy this single belt, though most remain far too small to observe without a sufficiently powerful telescope, and their combined mass is still considerably less than the mass of Earth's own moon, a striking illustration of just how small most individual asteroids actually are.

Many people mistakenly conflate asteroids with comets, yet these represent fundamentally different categories of celestial objects. Asteroids consist predominantly of solid rock and metal, with very little ice, whereas comets are composed primarily of ice mixed with dust, often described informally as dirty snowballs; when a comet travels sufficiently close to the sun, its ice vaporizes rapidly, producing a long, glowing tail of gas and dust that stretches dramatically behind it, while asteroids almost never develop a tail of this kind, since they simply lack sufficient ice to vaporize in such a manner.

Some asteroids eventually drift out of the main belt entirely, and a number of these, formally classified as near-Earth objects, can approach dangerously close to Earth's own orbital path; astronomers worldwide operate dedicated survey programs with powerful telescopes to continuously track these wandering bodies, calculating their precise orbits years or even decades before any potential close approach.

Though asteroids may appear small and rather unremarkable from a considerable distance, they teach scientists a tremendous amount about the solar system's distant past, since their material has remained largely unchanged for billions of years since the solar system itself first formed, offering scientists a rare and valuable glimpse of the raw material from which the rocky planets, including our own Earth, were originally assembled long ago, making asteroids invaluable time capsules from the dawn of our cosmic neighborhood.

MID.prompt: Imagine you are an astronomer explaining asteroids to a younger student. Write a short explanation of three facts that show how asteroids are different from comets.
checklist: I included three facts from the article comparing asteroids and comets.
I explained each fact in my own words.
I organized my explanation with an opening and a closing sentence.
MID.modelAnswer: Although people often mix up asteroids and comets, they are actually quite different objects in space. First, asteroids are made mostly of rock and metal, while comets are made mostly of ice mixed with dust. Second, when a comet gets close to the sun, its ice vaporizes and creates a long, glowing tail, but asteroids almost never form a tail because they contain so little ice. Third, most asteroids stay together in the crowded asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, while comets often travel on very different paths through the solar system. Understanding these differences helps scientists study each type of object in the right way.

HIGH.prompt: Explain, using evidence from the article, why asteroids are considered rocky leftovers from the solar system's formation, and describe how they differ from comets.
checklist: I explained why asteroids are considered leftover material using evidence from the article.
I clearly described at least two differences between asteroids and comets.
I organized my writing with a clear introduction, body, and conclusion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Asteroids are considered rocky leftovers from the solar system's formation because they are fragments of rock and metal that never grew large enough to become full planets. According to the article, billions of years ago countless fragments tried to clump together under gravity, but Jupiter's gravitational influence likely scattered many of them before they could merge, leaving them as the smaller, irregularly shaped bodies we now call asteroids. This is quite different from comets, which are composed mainly of ice mixed with dust rather than solid rock and metal. Because comets contain so much ice, their surfaces vaporize when they travel close to the sun, producing the long, glowing tails comets are famous for, while asteroids almost never form a tail since they simply lack that ice. In conclusion, asteroids and comets may both be leftover material from the early solar system, but their different compositions make them behave in very different ways.
